porfirio-d-az.name: Porfirio Díaz
porfirio-d-az.summary: Mexican army general and politician who ruled as dictator from 1876 to 1911, serving over thirty years as president, the longest of any Mexican ruler.

francisco-bulnes.name: Francisco Bulnes
francisco-bulnes.summary: Mexican scientist, journalist and politician (1847–1924), among the Científicos who backed President Porfirio Díaz, and later a critic of the Mexican Revolution.

second-french-intervention-in-mexico.name: French intervention in Mexico
second-french-intervention-in-mexico.summary: A French invasion of Mexico from 1861 to 1867 under Napoleon III, backed by Mexican conservatives, that installed Archduke Maximilian as emperor before the monarchy collapsed.

maximilian-i-of-mexico.name: Maximilian I of Mexico
maximilian-i-of-mexico.summary: Austrian archduke and younger brother of Emperor Franz Joseph I who became emperor of the Second Mexican Empire from 1864 until his execution in 1867.

porfiriato.name: Porfiriato
porfiriato.summary: The period when General Porfirio Díaz ruled Mexico, from 1876 until his fall in 1910, first as elected president and later as an authoritarian dictator pursuing 'order and progress.'

cuauht-moc.name: Cuauhtémoc
cuauht-moc.summary: The last Aztec emperor, ruling Tenochtitlan from 1520 to 1521 while it was besieged by the Spanish and struck by smallpox; his name means 'Descending Eagle'.

paseo-de-la-reforma.name: Paseo de la Reforma
paseo-de-la-reforma.summary: A wide diagonal avenue in Mexico City, designed for Emperor Maximilian in the 1860s and modeled on European boulevards like Vienna's Ringstraße and the Champs-Élysées.

adamo-boari.name: Adamo Boari
adamo-boari.summary: Italian Art Nouveau and Art Deco engineer and architect (1863–1928) known for notable Historicist buildings built in Mexico.

palacio-de-bellas-artes.name: Palacio de Bellas Artes
palacio-de-bellas-artes.summary: Mexico City's main centre for performing and visual arts, begun in 1904 for the 1910 independence centennial but not completed until 1934 after construction problems.

angel-of-independence.name: Angel of Independence
angel-of-independence.summary: A victory column in Mexico City, built in 1910 to mark the centennial of Mexico's War of Independence and later turned into a mausoleum for the war's heroes.

christopher-columbus.name: Christopher Columbus
christopher-columbus.summary: Italian explorer and navigator (1451–1506) whose four Spanish-sponsored voyages opened the way for European exploration and colonization of the Americas.

juan-cordero.name: Juan Cordero
juan-cordero.summary: Mexican painter and muralist (1822–1884) in the Classical style who began his career in Rome and Florence, Italy.

santa-teresa-la-antigua.name: Santa Teresa la Antigua
santa-teresa-la-antigua.summary: A former convent in the historic center of Mexico City, near the main plaza, that stopped operating as a convent in the late 19th century and now houses an alternative art center.

gabino-barreda.name: Gabino Barreda
gabino-barreda.summary: Mexican doctor, philosopher and politician (1818–1881) who introduced French positivism to Mexican education and founded the National Preparatory School under President Juárez.

monument-to-cuauht-moc.name: Monument to Cuauhtémoc
monument-to-cuauht-moc.summary: An 1887 monument in Mexico City honoring Cuauhtémoc, the last Mexica ruler of Tenochtitlan, commissioned to promote Porfirio Díaz's government.

benito-ju-rez.name: Benito Juárez
benito-ju-rez.summary: Mexican politician and lawyer, president of Mexico from 1858 to 1872 and the country's first Indigenous president, who led Liberal victories in the Reform War and against French intervention.

mitla.name: Mitla
mitla.summary: The main religious center of the Zapotec, near Oaxaca, Mexico, known for elaborate mosaic stonework on tombs and walls; later influenced by the Mixtec.

national-palace-mexico.name: National Palace
national-palace-mexico.summary: Seat of Mexico's federal government on Mexico City's main square, built partly from the original palace of Aztec-era ruler Moctezuma II, and the president's official residence since 2018.

jeremy-bentham.name: Jeremy Bentham
jeremy-bentham.summary: An English philosopher and jurist (1748–1832) regarded as the founder of modern utilitarianism, who argued for the greatest happiness of the greatest number and advocated abolishing slavery and capital punishment.

panopticon.name: Panopticon
panopticon.summary: An 18th-century prison design by philosopher Jeremy Bentham allowing a single guard to observe all inmates without them knowing when they're watched, encouraging self-regulation.

ni-os-h-roes.name: Niños Héroes
ni-os-h-roes.summary: Six Mexican military cadets killed defending Mexico City at the Battle of Chapultepec in 1847, now honored on a Mexican civic holiday.

chapultepec.name: Chapultepec
chapultepec.summary: A large forested park in Mexico City centered on Chapultepec Hill, a retreat for Aztec rulers and later home to Chapultepec Castle.

caste-war-of-yucat-n.name: Caste War of Yucatán
caste-war-of-yucat-n.summary: An 1847–1915 revolt of Indigenous Maya people in Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula against Hispanic control, considered one of the most successful modern Native American uprisings.

battle-of-molino-del-rey.name: Battle of Molino del Rey
battle-of-molino-del-rey.summary: An 8 September 1847 battle near Mexico City, one of the bloodiest of the Mexican-American War, fought between Mexican forces under Antonio León and Americans under Winfield Scott.

battle-of-chapultepec.name: Battle of Chapultepec
battle-of-chapultepec.summary: An 1847 battle in which U.S. troops captured Chapultepec Castle outside Mexico City during the Mexican–American War, opening the way to the capital's fall; remembered in Mexico for the young cadets who died defending it.

winfield-scott.name: Winfield Scott
winfield-scott.summary: Winfield Scott: American military commander (1786–1866) who served in the Mexican–American War and as Commanding General of the Army from 1841 to 1861.

miguel-hidalgo-y-costilla.name: Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla
miguel-hidalgo-y-costilla.summary: A Mexican Catholic priest who launched the Mexican War of Independence with his 1810 Cry of Dolores and is honored as the Father of the Nation.

grito-de-dolores.name: Cry of Dolores
grito-de-dolores.summary: The call to arms given by priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla on 16 September 1810 that triggered the Mexican War of Independence.

jos-mar-a-morelos.name: José María Morelos
jos-mar-a-morelos.summary: Catholic priest and military leader who led the Mexican War of Independence after Hidalgo's 1811 execution, wrote the Sentimientos de la Nación, and declared independence at the Congress of Anáhuac before being captured and executed in 1815.

vicente-guerrero.name: Vicente Guerrero
vicente-guerrero.summary: A Mexican guerrilla commander and statesman who joined the independence insurgency in 1810, kept resistance alive from 1816 to 1821, and became Mexico's second president in 1829.

chapultepec-castle.name: Chapultepec Castle
chapultepec-castle.summary: A castle atop Chapultepec Hill in Mexico City, built as a colonial viceroy's summer house, later home to Emperor Maximilian I and Mexican presidents until becoming a museum in 1939.

nicol-s-bravo.name: Nicolás Bravo
nicol-s-bravo.summary: Mexican soldier and politician (1786–1854) who served as interim president three times and fought in both the war of independence and the war with the US.

antonio-l-pez-de-santa-anna.name: Antonio López de Santa Anna
antonio-l-pez-de-santa-anna.summary: Mexican general and politician (1794–1876) who served as president of Mexico multiple times between 1833 and 1855, a dominant and controversial figure blamed for the loss of Mexican territory to the United States.

treaty-of-guadalupe-hidalgo.name: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
treaty-of-guadalupe-hidalgo.summary: Negotiated by U.S. envoy Nicholas Trist, it let Mexicans in the annexed territory choose relocation or American citizenship, and was ratified by the Senate over Whig opposition.

juan-de-la-barrera.name: Juan de la Barrera
juan-de-la-barrera.summary: A Mexican military cadet (1828–1847) who died defending Chapultepec Castle during the Mexican–American War; one of the six Niños Héroes revered for their bravery.

heroic-military-academy.name: Heroic Military College
heroic-military-academy.summary: Mexico's major military educational institution, founded in 1823 in Mexico City; famed as the school of the Niños Héroes, the cadets who died defending it in 1847.

william-j-worth.name: William J. Worth
william-j-worth.summary: American army officer (1794–1849) who served in the War of 1812, the Second Seminole War and the Mexican–American War.

british-honduras.name: British Honduras
british-honduras.summary: British Crown colony on the southern Yucatán Peninsula from 1783 to 1964, renamed Belize in 1973 and gaining full independence in 1981.

chan-santa-cruz.name: Chan Santa Cruz
chan-santa-cruz.summary: A late 19th-century independent Maya state, also called the Maya Free State, centered on a shrine in what is now Quintana Roo, Mexico, that gave rise to the Cruzoob religious movement.

isidro-barrada.name: Isidro Barradas
isidro-barrada.summary: Isidro Barrada: A Spanish general (1782–1835) sent to Mexico in 1829 in an unsuccessful attempt to reconquer the country for Spain, eight years after Mexican independence.

isabella-ii.name: Isabella II
isabella-ii.summary: Queen of Spain from 1833 until her deposition in 1868, the only queen regnant in the history of unified Spain.

p-g-t-beauregard.name: P. G. T. Beauregard
p-g-t-beauregard.summary: American military officer, trained as an engineer, who later became the Confederate general who started the American Civil War at Fort Sumter in 1861.

gertrudis-g-mez-de-avellaneda.name: Gertrudis Gómez de Avellaneda
gertrudis-g-mez-de-avellaneda.summary: Cuban-born Spanish writer (1814–1873) best known for her 1841 antislavery novel Sab, about a slave in love with his unaware mistress.

cirilo-villaverde.name: Cirilo Villaverde
cirilo-villaverde.summary: Cuban poet, novelist, journalist and freedom fighter (1812–1894), best known for his novel Cecilia Valdés about class and race in colonial Cuba.

jos-mar-a-heredia-y-heredia.name: José María Heredia
jos-mar-a-heredia-y-heredia.summary: Cuban-born poet (1803–1839) regarded as the first romantic poet of the Americas, exiled for pro-independence activity and later a naturalized Mexican citizen.

jos-mart.name: José Martí
jos-mart.summary: Cuban writer, philosopher, and political activist (1853–1895) who campaigned for Cuban independence from Spain and became a symbol of that cause, known as the 'Apostle of Cuban Independence.'

cholula-mesoamerican-site.name: Cholula
cholula-mesoamerican-site.summary: A pre-Columbian Mesoamerican city near modern Puebla, Mexico, and a key religious center home to the largest pyramid structure by volume in the world.

juan-clemente-zenea.name: Juan Clemente Zenea
juan-clemente-zenea.summary: Cuban writer born in 1832, credited with reintroducing Romanticism to Cuban literature and marking a new age in Hispano-American poetry; he campaigned in exile against Spanish rule.

luisa-p-rez-de-zambrana.name: Luisa Pérez de Zambrana
luisa-p-rez-de-zambrana.summary: A Cuban writer and translator (1837-1922), regarded as one of Cuba's greatest poets.

cecilia-vald-s.name: Cecilia Valdés
cecilia-vald-s.summary: An 1882 novel by Cuban writer Cirilo Villaverde, notable for depicting the interaction of classes and races in Havana, Cuba.

ram-n-meza-y-su-rez-incl-n.name: Ramón Meza
ram-n-meza-y-su-rez-incl-n.summary: Cuban literary critic, historian and professor at the University of Havana (1861–1911), who wrote works of both fiction and non-fiction.

claudio-linati.name: Claudio Linati
claudio-linati.summary: Italian painter and lithographer (1790–1832) who set up Mexico's first lithographic press and co-founded a periodical with Mexico's first political cartoons.

jean-fr-d-ric-waldeck.name: Jean-Frédéric Waldeck
jean-fr-d-ric-waldeck.summary: A French antiquarian, cartographer, artist and explorer (c. 1766 – c. 1875) known for exploring Mexico and publishing drawings of Maya and Aztec sculpture, though much of his life is unverified.

second-mexican-empire.name: Second Mexican Empire
second-mexican-empire.summary: A constitutional monarchy established in Mexico from 1864 with French backing, ruled by Austrian Archduke Maximilian, that collapsed after French military support was withdrawn.

valent-n-g-mez-far-as.name: Valentín Gómez Farías
valent-n-g-mez-far-as.summary: Mexican doctor and liberal politician (1781-1858) who served twice as president of Mexico and pursued anti-clerical reforms limiting the Church's power.

carl-sofus-lumholtz.name: Carl Sofus Lumholtz
carl-sofus-lumholtz.summary: Norwegian explorer and ethnographer (1851–1922) known for detailed field research and publications on indigenous cultures of Australia and Mexico.

rar-muri.name: Rarámuri (Tarahumara)
rar-muri.summary: Indigenous people of Chihuahua, Mexico, known for long-distance running as prayer, who retreated into the Sierra Madre's canyons after 16th-century Spanish colonization.

transit-of-venus.name: Transit of Venus
transit-of-venus.summary: A rare astronomical event in which Venus passes across the face of the Sun, historically used to calculate the distance from Earth to Venus and the scale of the solar system.

royal-and-pontifical-university-of-mexic.name: Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico
royal-and-pontifical-university-of-mexic.summary: A university founded in 1551 by royal decree of Charles I of Spain, among the earliest in North America; repeatedly closed and reopened amid conflicts between liberals and the Church, before abolition in 1865.
royal-and-pontifical-university-of-mexic.source_title: Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico

first-mexican-empire.name: First Mexican Empire
first-mexican-empire.summary: Constitutional monarchy and first independent government of Mexico, existing from 1821 to 1823 under Emperor Agustín I.

napoleon-iii.name: Napoleon III
napoleon-iii.summary: Nephew of Napoleon I, first elected President of France (1848–1852) then Emperor of the French until 1870, when he was captured by Prussia and its allies at the Battle of Sedan.

plan-of-iguala.name: Plan of Iguala
plan-of-iguala.summary: A proclamation issued on 24 February 1821 near the end of the Mexican War of Independence, calling for a constitutional monarchy with equal rights for Spanish- and Mexican-born citizens.

agust-n-de-iturbide.name: Agustín de Iturbide
agust-n-de-iturbide.summary: A Mexican army officer who led the final campaign for independence in 1821 and became the first Emperor of Mexico in 1822, abdicating the following year.

charlotte-of-belgium.name: Carlota
charlotte-of-belgium.summary: Belgian princess (1840–1927) who married Maximilian of Austria and became Empress of Mexico from 1864; she ruled as regent during his absences, making her the first woman to rule in the Americas.

spanish-constitution-of-1812.name: Spanish Constitution of 1812
spanish-constitution-of-1812.summary: Spain's first constitution, ratified in 1812, which affirmed national sovereignty, separation of powers and a constitutional monarchy while keeping Catholicism as the sole official religion.

army-of-the-three-guarantees.name: Army of the Three Guarantees
army-of-the-three-guarantees.summary: Combined Spanish royalist and Mexican insurgent army formed at the end of the Mexican War of Independence to defend the guarantees of religion, independence and unity.

pope-pius-ix.name: Pope Pius IX
pope-pius-ix.summary: Head of the Catholic Church from 1846 to 1878, the longest verified reign of any pope, who lost the Papal States to the Kingdom of Italy in 1870 and declared himself a prisoner in the Vatican.

mexican-railway.name: Imperial Mexican Railway Company
mexican-railway.summary: A British-incorporated company set up in 1864 to build a railway in Mexico, later renamed the Mexican Railway in 1867 after French forces withdrew.

sebasti-n-lerdo-de-tejada.name: Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada
sebasti-n-lerdo-de-tejada.summary: Mexican liberal politician and jurist who served as the 31st president of Mexico from 1872 to 1876, succeeding Benito Juárez before being overthrown by Porfirio Díaz.

palo-religion.name: Palo
palo-religion.summary: An African diasporic religion developed in Cuba in the late 19th or early 20th century, drawing on Kongo religious tradition alongside Catholic and Spiritist influences, centered on spirits of the dead.

ngola-title.name: Ngola
ngola-title.summary: The title of the king of the Kingdom of Ndongo, in what is now north-west Angola, from the 16th to 17th century; the country of Angola is named after it.

kingdom-of-kongo.name: Kingdom of Kongo
kingdom-of-kongo.summary: A Central African kingdom spanning parts of modern Angola, Congo and Gabon, independent from around 1390 to 1862, later a Portuguese vassal until its monarchy was abolished in 1914.

charles-tienne-brasseur-de-bourbourg.name: Brasseur de Bourbourg
charles-tienne-brasseur-de-bourbourg.summary: French priest and scholar (1814–1874) who specialized in Mesoamerican studies; his speculative theories linking the Maya to Atlantis helped inspire the pseudo-science of Mayanism.

james-thomson-pastor.name: James Diego Thomson
james-thomson-pastor.summary: Scottish Baptist pastor and educator (1788–1854) who worked as a schoolmaster in South America, introducing the Lancasterian teaching system there.

british-and-foreign-bible-society.name: British and Foreign Bible Society
british-and-foreign-bible-society.summary: Non-denominational Christian Bible society founded in 1804 by William Wilberforce and others to encourage wider circulation and use of the Bible worldwide.

amado-nervo.name: Amado Nervo
amado-nervo.summary: Mexican poet, journalist and educator (1870-1919) known for mystical, metaphor-rich poetry blending Christianity and Hinduism, considered one of the 19th century's most important Mexican poets.

nzambi-ampungu.name: Nzambi Ampungu
nzambi-ampungu.summary: The Supreme God and eternal Sky Father of traditional Kongo spirituality, associated with the sun; his female counterpart rules the moon. After Portuguese colonization he became identified with the Christian God.

nganga.name: Nganga
nganga.summary: A spiritual healer, diviner and ritual specialist in traditional Kongo religion, also found among descendants of Kongo and Mbundu peoples across the African diaspora, including Brazil, Cuba and Haiti.

alexander-von-humboldt.name: Alexander von Humboldt
alexander-von-humboldt.summary: A German polymath, geographer and explorer (1769–1859) who traveled extensively through the Americas from 1799 to 1804 and helped found modern geography.

antiquities-of-mexico.name: Antiquities of Mexico
antiquities-of-mexico.summary: A 19th-century compilation of facsimile reproductions of Mesoamerican codices and historical accounts, published in nine volumes by Lord Kingsborough between 1831 and 1846.

augustus-le-plongeon.name: Augustus Le Plongeon
augustus-le-plongeon.summary: British-American antiquarian and photographer (1825–1908) who studied and photographed Maya ruins in the Yucatán and promoted Mayanism.

ignatius-l-donnelly.name: Ignatius L. Donnelly
ignatius-l-donnelly.summary: An American congressman and populist writer (1831–1901) best known for fringe theories about Atlantis, ancient catastrophic impacts, and Shakespearean authorship, now regarded as pseudoscience.

atlantis-the-antediluvian-world.name: Atlantis: The Antediluvian World
atlantis-the-antediluvian-world.summary: An 1882 pseudoarchaeological book by Ignatius L. Donnelly arguing that Plato's Atlantis was real and that all ancient civilizations descended from it.

alcides-arguedas.name: Alcides Arguedas
alcides-arguedas.summary: Bolivian writer and historian (1879–1946) whose 1919 novel Raza de bronce shaped Bolivian thought on national identity and indigenous affairs.

jos-vasconcelos.name: José Vasconcelos
jos-vasconcelos.summary: Mexican writer, philosopher, lawyer and politician (1882–1959) called the 'cultural caudillo' of the Mexican Revolution, whose 'cosmic race' philosophy shaped modern Mexican society, politics and economic policy.

la-raza-c-smica.name: La raza cósmica
la-raza-c-smica.summary: A 1925 Spanish-language book by Mexican philosopher José Vasconcelos arguing for a future 'cosmic race' blending all the world's peoples into a new civilization.

palacio-de-correos-de-m-xico.name: Palacio de Correos de México
palacio-de-correos-de-m-xico.summary: Mexico City's ornate main post office building, completed in 1907 in an eclectic Neo-Plateresque style and later restored after damage from the 1985 earthquake.

jaime-nun.name: Jaime Nunó
jaime-nun.summary: Spanish composer from Catalonia (1824–1908) who composed the music for the Mexican national anthem.

conservatorio-nacional-de-m-sica-mexico.name: National Conservatory of Music
conservatorio-nacional-de-m-sica-mexico.summary: A music conservatory located in Mexico City, Mexico.

cueca.name: Cueca
cueca.summary: A family of couple dances and music, danced with a handkerchief, dating to the late 18th century and now the national dance of Chile.

cenobio-paniagua.name: Cenobio Paniagua
cenobio-paniagua.summary: A Mexican musician and composer (1821–1882) known for his romantic operas and religious music.

felice-romani.name: Felice Romani
felice-romani.summary: An Italian poet and scholar (1788–1865) who wrote many opera librettos for composers Donizetti and Bellini, ranked among Italy's finest librettists.

aniceto-ortega.name: Aniceto Ortega del Villar
aniceto-ortega.summary: A Mexican doctor, composer and pianist (1825 to 1875), remembered for his 1871 opera Guatimotzin, one of the earliest Mexican operas on a native subject.

guatimotzin.name: Guatimotzin
guatimotzin.summary: An 1871 Mexican opera by Aniceto Ortega del Villar, based on the defense of Mexico by its last Aztec ruler, Cuauhtémoc.

mar-a-uicab.name: María Uicab
mar-a-uicab.summary: 19th-century Maya priestess and leader nicknamed the 'Queen of Tulum,' influential in the Cruzoob religious movement during the Caste War of Yucatán; the end of her life remains a mystery.

tulum.name: Tulum
tulum.summary: A walled pre-Columbian Maya city on cliffs along Mexico's Caribbean coast, a major port for Coba that reached its height in the 13th to 15th centuries and was still inhabited decades after Spanish contact.
